summary: Lists the requirements for an IETF toolset that would help people submit, validate, and publish Internet-Drafts. It is a planning document that says what such tools should do, rather than a protocol specification.

eli5.summary: This is a wish list for a website where people hand in their draft documents. It says how the site should check homework and put it on the shelf.

questions: how do you submit internet draft to ietf
what checks internet draft before posting
automatic validation of internet draft format
subtitle: A web-based system to streamline submitting Internet-Drafts for review.

tldr.problem: IETF participants submit thousands of drafts per year, but manual handling by the Secretariat creates delays, backlogs, and limits quality checking of submissions.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies requirements for an automated toolset that accepts drafts from submitters, validates their format and metadata, and posts valid ones immediately to the IETF repository without Secretariat review.
tldr.outcome: Authors no longer wait days for draft posting; errors are caught upfront rather than by RFC Editor; and the Secretariat can focus on edge cases instead of routine approval.

today: RFC 4228 is an Informational RFC documenting requirements for an IETF tools system. The IETF has since developed automated draft submission systems that follow these or similar requirements, making the manual Secretariat review process much faster.

sections.title: The Problem with Manual Submission
sections.content:
The IETF publishes thousands of Internet-Drafts every year (7,000 in 2004 alone). Each one must be submitted to the IETF Secretariat via email, reviewed by hand, and approved or rejected. This manual process has consequences: submissions may wait hours or days for review; postings bunch up in batches every 4 hours; and during IETF meetings, the backlog becomes weeks long.

The Secretariat checks submissions against a short checklist, but does not validate them against IETF publishing rules in detail. As a result, authors do not find out about problems until the RFC Editor points them out later. Quality issues also go uncaught, reducing the usefulness of Internet-Drafts and increasing the RFC Editor's workload.
sections.eli5: It takes the teacher days to grade homework and say whether it is accepted. By then, students may have given up and posted the homework somewhere else online.

sections.title: How the Toolset Would Work
sections.content:
Instead of emailing the draft, an author uploads it to a web page. The system extracts metadata (title, authors, version number), validates the format and content against IETF rules, and displays the results. If everything passes, the author clicks to post immediately. If there are errors, the author can fix the draft and resubmit, or ask the Secretariat to review it by hand.

The workflow has three paths: (1) automatic posting if validation passes; (2) asking the Secretariat for manual review if there are problems; or (3) canceling. The toolset also provides an email interface for authors who prefer not to use the web.

Submissions have a session timeout. If an author abandons their submission without canceling it, the toolset cleans it up after one hour (or longer if waiting for approval).
sections.eli5: You upload the homework, the website checks it in a few seconds, and says yes or no. If yes, it is posted right away. If no, you see what went wrong and can try again.

sections.title: What the Toolset Checks
sections.content:
The toolset validates submissions against two categories of rules. Absolute requirements prevent posting: the metadata must match across all formats (plain text, XML, PDF); the version number must be correct; the draft must have an IETF intellectual property statement; the creation date must be recent (within 3 days); and expiration must follow IETF rules.

For version 00 of a Working Group draft, the toolset also checks for approval from the WG Chair. This can happen before or after submission; if not yet received, the system can wait for it.

Desirable features trigger warnings but do not block posting: the toolset checks for formatting issues using external tools (the idnits checker from the IETF); warns if the draft is unexpectedly a new version (e.g., posting version 05 when WGs rarely update so frequently); and if both XML and plain text are submitted, verifies they represent the same document.
sections.eli5: Some mistakes are deal-breakers: wrong version number, no legal statement, authors do not match. Others are just yellow flags: messy formatting, confusing choices. The website tells you which is which.

sections.title: Who Can Post
sections.content:
Not just anyone can post a draft. The toolset checks whether the submitter is authorized. For version 00 of a new draft, anyone can submit (the author is assumed to be the submitter). For version N+1 of an existing draft, only someone listed as an author of version N can post it. For a WG-named draft, only the WG Chair or an IESG member can post it. For individual drafts, any author or an IESG member can post.

The toolset authenticates the submitter by sending a login token to their email address and requiring them to use it to prove they have access to that email. More sophisticated authentication (client certificates, PGP signatures) is listed as a future enhancement.
sections.eli5: You can only post your own homework or your group's homework. The website sends a secret code to your email to prove it is really you.

sections.title: Key Design Goals
sections.content:
The toolset is designed to be robust, transparent, and maintainable. It must handle multiple authors submitting the same draft simultaneously or one author submitting many drafts at once. It stores submitted drafts and metadata in a staging area so authors can correct and resubmit without losing their work.

The toolset must defend against denial-of-service attacks (e.g., someone uploading thousands of tiny drafts). It sets daily thresholds: no more than 3 versions of the same draft per day, no more than 10 versions from the same submitter per day, and 400 versions total per day. These limits protect the repository from being overwhelmed while still allowing legitimate use.

All source code should be publicly available under an open-source license, with a public bug tracker and discussion forum. This allows the IETF community to review the code, report issues, and even contribute improvements.
sections.eli5: The website should not break if ten people upload at once or if someone tries to spam it with a thousand fake drafts. The code should be public so anyone can check that it is honest.
